abstract: Intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR) is associated with increased risk of cardiometabolic disease later in life and has been shown to affect female and male offspring differently, but the mechanisms remain unclear. The purpose of this study was to identify proteomic differences and metabolic risk markers in IUGR male and female neonates when compared to appropriate for gestational age (AGA) babies that will provide a better understanding of IUGR pathogenesis and its associated risks. Our results revealed alterations in IUGR cord plasma proteomes with most of the differentially abundant proteins implicated in peroxisome pathways. This effect was evident in females but not in males. Furthermore, we observed that catalase activity, a peroxisomal enzyme, was significantly increased in females ( p < 0.05) but unchanged in males. Finally, we identified risk proteins associated with obesity, type-2 diabetes, and glucose intolerance such as EGF containing fibulin extracellular matrix protein 1 (EFEMP1), proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9 (PCSK9) and transforming growth factor beta receptor 3 (TGFBR3) proteins unique to females while coagulation factor IX (C9) and retinol binding protein 4 (RBP4) are unique in males. In conclusion, IUGR may display sexual dimorphism which may be associated with differences in lifelong risk for cardiometabolic disease between males and females.

MATERIAL AND METHODS
2.1 |
Study subjects—Cohort descriptions
Neonates of pregnant women who received prenatal care and delivered at a large urban, private, non-profit hospital in Bronx, New York, were enrolled in the study. Inclusion criteria included healthy term, appropriate for gestational age (AGA) or intrauterine growth restricted (IUGR) singleton neonates born to mothers with no prenatal history of depression, smoking during the second or third trimesters of pregnancy, or gestational/type 2 diabetes. Infants who were large for gestational age, and those with an Apgar score <7 at 5 min of age, chromosomal/congenital abnormalities, congenital infections, or inborn errors of metabolism were excluded. A total of 21 cord plasma samples from IUGR cases and 70 from AGA controls were used for the study. Venous cord blood samples were collected. Maternal and infant characteristics of the 91 participants are summarized in
Table 1
.
2.2 |
Ethics statement
This study was approved by the Montefiore Medical Center/Albert Einstein College of Medicine Institutional Review Board (
NCT03402139
). A written informed consent was obtained from all participants prior to study-related activities and procedures.
2.3 |
Sample collection and plasma preparation
Umbilical cord blood was collected during labor or cesarean section after delivery of the placenta. Samples were placed in CPDA-anticoagulant blood bag. Plasma was obtained by centrifugation at 3000 rpm for 15 min at 4°C and samples were stored at 80°C for further use.
2.4 |
Proteomic analysis
2.4.1 |
S-trap protein digestion
Hundred microliter of plasma per sample was resuspended in 5% SDS 50 mM ammonium bicarbonate and 5 mM DTT and incubated for 30 min at 60°C. Samples were then alkylated with 20 mM iodoacetamide in the dark for 30 min. Afterward, phosphoric acid was added to the sample at a final concentration of 1.2%. Samples were diluted in six volumes of binding buffer (90% methanol and 10 mM ammonium bicarbonate, pH 8.0). After gentle mixing, the protein solution was loaded to a 96-well S-Trap
™
plate (Protifi) and spun at 500 g for 30 s. The sample was washed twice with binding buffer. Finally, 1 μg of sequencing grade trypsin (Promega), diluted in 50 mM ammonium bicarbonate, was added into the 96-well S-Trap
™
plate and samples were digested at 37°C for 18 h. Peptides were eluted in three steps: (i) 40 μL of 50 mM ammonium bicarbonate, (ii) 40 μL of 0.1% Trifluoroacetic acid (TFA) and (iii) 40 μL of 60% acetonitrile and 0.1% TFA. The peptide solution was pooled, spun at 1000 g for 30 s, and dried in a vacuum centrifuge.
2.4.2 |
Sample desalting
Prior to mass spectrometry analysis, samples were desalted using a 96-well plate filter (Orochem) packed with 1 mg of Oasis HLB C-18 resin (Waters). Briefly, the samples were resuspended in 100 μL of 0.1% TFA and loaded onto the HLB resin, which was previously equilibrated using 100 μL of the same buffer. After washing with 100 μL of 0.1% TFA, the samples were eluted with a buffer containing 70 μL of 60% acetonitrile and 0.1% TFA and then dried in a vacuum centrifuge.
2.4.3 |
LC-MS/MS acquisition and analysis
Samples were resuspended in 10 μL of 0.1% TFA and loaded onto a Dionex RSLC Ultimate 3000 (Thermo Scientific), coupled online with an Orbitrap Fusion Lumos (Thermo Scientific). Chromatographic separation was performed with a two-column system, consisting of a C-18 trap PepMap
™
Neo Trap Cartridge (300 μm ID, 5 mm length, product number 174500) and a picofrit analytical column (75 μm ID, 25 cm length, in-house packed using Dr. Maisch C18-AQ bulk resin, 3 μm size, product number r13.aq). Peptides were separated using a 120 min gradient from 4% to 30% buffer B (buffer A: 0.1% formic acid, buffer B: 80% acetonitrile + 0.1% formic acid) at a flow rate of 300 nL/min. The mass spectrometer was set to acquire spectra in a data-dependent acquisition (DDA) mode. Briefly, the full MS scan was set to 300–1200
m
/
z
in the orbitrap with a resolution of 120,000 (at 200
m
/
z
) and an AGC target of 5 × 10e5. MS/MS was performed in the ion trap using the top speed mode (2 s), which is the maximum cycle time for MS/MS acquisition prior to return to Full MS acquisition. The MS/MS AGC target was set to 1 × 10e4 and the HCD collision energy was set at 35 (normalized). Dynamic exclusion was set to 45 s. Precursor fit was enabled. Charge state selection was set to 2–6. Monoisotopic precursor selection was set to “Peptide” mode. Intensity threshold for selection of signals for MS/MS was set to 1 × 10e4.
Proteome raw files were searched using Proteome Discoverer software (v2.4, Thermo Scientific) using SEQUEST search engine and the SwissProt human database (updated June 2021). The search for total proteome included variable modification of N-terminal acetylation, and fixed modification of carbamidomethyl cysteine. Trypsin was specified as the digestive enzyme with up to two missed cleavages allowed. Mass tolerance was set to 10 ppm for precursor ions and 0.2 Da for product ions. Peptide and protein false discovery rate were set to 1%. For quantification, we used the Minora Feature Detector algorithm for signal extraction, the Feature Mapper for chromatographic alignment, and the Precursor Ions Quantifier for quantifying proteins. In this last, we utilized only unique and razor peptides for protein quantification, and we utilized the top three average setting for inferring protein abundance from peptide intensities [
19
].
2.5 |
Bioinformatics analysis
Gene ontology (GO) term enrichment analysis was carried out using GOrilla program [
20
]. GOrilla employs a flexible threshold statistical approach to discover GO terms significantly enriched at the top of a ranked list of genes and computes an exact
p
-value according to the mHG or HG model. To calculate the GO enrichment, we selected in GOrilla “Single ranked list of genes”. This way, the software calculates the enrichment based on how the gene names (or UniProt protein accession numbers) are sorted in the input box. To sort proteins prior to the enrichment, we used an arbitrary “score” calculated by multiplying the log2 fold change ratio and the −log2 t-test
p
-value. The single ranked gene lists were submitted as inputs to GOrilla server at:
http://cbl-gorilla.cs.technion.ac.il
with default running parameters.
STRING (version 11.5) analysis was performed to identify possible interaction networks among the proteins. Threshold for confidence was set to medium and the STRING networks were visualized with Cytoscape (version 3.9.1).
2.6 |
Catalase activity
Catalase enzyme activity was measured in cord plasma in a subset of randomly picked study participants [IUGR,
n
= 16 (female
n
= 10 and male
n
= 6) and AGA,
n
= 19 (female
n
= 10 and male
n
= 9)] according to the manufacturer’s protocol using a colorimetric kit (Cayman chemical, Michigan). Student’s
t
-test and one-way ANOVA were used to assess statistical significance.
2.7 |
Statistical and regression analysis
Statistical analysis was performed using Student’s
t
test, one-way and two-way ANOVA as indicated with SPSS 29.0 (SPSS Inc., Chicago, IL, USA). Differences were considered significant when
p
< 0.05.
Based on our data and literature review, we compared the following proteins: CAT, AKR1B1, IDH1, GLRX, MMP2, and PAPPA2 between IUGR and AGA using univariable linear regression. We then performed multivariable linear regression modeling with adjustment for infant sex, ethnicity, preeclampsia (PE)/hypertension (HTN), and pre-pregnancy BMI because these variables have both biological and clinical relevance.

Supplementary Material
Supplemental material file
SUPPORTING INFORMATION
Additional supporting information may be found online
https://doi.org/10.1002/pmic.202300260
in the Supporting Information section at the end of the article.

INTRODUCTION
Intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR) is a condition in which the fetus fails to reach its genetically determined growth potential. It affects approximately 5%–7% of pregnancies in the US [
1
,
2
] and is one of the leading causes of perinatal mortality and morbidity [
3
,
4
]. According to the developmental origin of health and disease hypothesis, adverse fetal development may have a lifelong impact on health [
5
] and IUGR increases risk of cardiometabolic disease and neurodevelopmental disorders later in life [
3
,
6
]. The primary cause of IUGR in developed countries is uteroplacental vascular insufficiency. A variety of maternal factors such as smoking, essential hypertension, preeclampsia, and diabetes mellitus, as well as fetal and genetic factors, also play a role [
3
].
Proteomic profiling can provide a deeper understanding of the pathogenesis of IUGR and identify potential therapeutic targets to prevent it. Several proteomic studies, related to IUGR, have focused on maternal and placental factors with very few studies on umbilical cord blood. Molecular profiling of maternal plasma have revealed alterations in lipid metabolism, activation of pro-coagulant, reactive oxygen species, nutrient transport, energy metabolism, and immune-mediated chronic inflammation pathways [
7
–
11
]. In the IUGR placental proteome, most detected proteins are related to oxidative stress, cellular oxidation and detoxication, apoptosis, angiogenesis, energy transduction, cell proliferation, differentiation, and intracellular signaling [
12
–
15
].
In addition, recent studies in human and animal models have demonstrated that IUGR can affect female and male offspring differently [
16
–
18
]. While it has been proposed that females have stronger adaptive strategies during fetal development than males, the mechanisms driving sex-dependent differences remain unclear. Hence, this study aims to characterize proteins in cord plasma from male and female IUGR infants to identify proteomic differences and metabolic risk markers that will extend our understanding of IUGR.

3 |
RESULTS
3.1 |
Identification of differentially abundant proteins in umbilical cord blood plasma between AGA and IUGR newborns as well as influence of sex
Using mass spectrometry, we identified 852 proteins in cord plasma, out of which 465 and 387 proteins were found to be more and less abundant, respectively, in IUGR compared with AGA. However, after stratifying based on sex, 521 and 331 proteins were found to be more and less abundant, respectively, in IUGR females whereas 375 and 477 proteins were found to be more and less abundant, respectively, in IUGR males.
Figure 1(A
–
C)
depicts the volcano plots of the 852 quantified proteins in IUGR as well as in IUGR males and females highlighting the top 10 proteins most regulated in red and less regulated in blue ranked based on an arbitrary score value calculated by multiplying the log2 fold change ratio and the −log2
t
-test
p
-value.
Using a two-way ANOVA analysis, we found 77 proteins were statistically significant (
p
< 0.05) in abundance between the IUGR versus AGA groups (growth only) out of which 62 and 15 were more and less abundant in IUGR, respectively (
Table 2
), 36 proteins were significantly different between males and females (sex only), and 29 proteins showed a significant interaction between growth and sex (
Tables S1
and
S2
, respectively).
Interestingly, based on sex stratification, 59 proteins were significantly differentially abundant in both IUGR females and males, out of which 46 and 13 were more and less abundant, respectively, in IUGR females whereas 13 and 46 were more and less abundant, respectively, in IUGR males (
Tables 3
and
4
).
3.2 |
GO enrichment analysis implicates the role of peroxisome in IUGR pathogenesis
Based on GO analysis, peroxisomal transport, organization, and localization as well as electron transport chain, nucleotide metabolic, and catabolic processes were enriched in IUGR (
Figure 2A
). Pathways associated with less abundant proteins in IUGR were predominantly involved in platelet degranulation and aggregation, cell adhesion and regulation of response to stimulus (
Figure 2B
).
Another finding of the GO analysis was that IUGR females were enriched in pregnancy, peroxisomal transport, organization, and localization as well as oxygen transport, monosaccharide, and glycosyl compound metabolic processes (
Figure 2C
), while pathways with less abundant proteins in IUGR females were predominantly involved in platelet degranulation and aggregation, cell-matrix adhesion, complement activation, and regulation of ERK1 and ERK2 cascade (
Figure 2D
). Interestingly, in IUGR males, no GO biological processes were significantly enriched when analyzing the list of proteins that exhibited higher abundances in IUGR subjects relative to AGA subjects. Proteins that displayed lower abundances in IUGR males are involved in positive regulation of peptidyl-tyrosine phosphorylation, LDL mediated signaling, and LPL particle mediated signaling (
Figure 2E
).
3.3 |
Network and clustering analysis of significant (
p
< 0.05) differentially abundant proteins
Using only the statistically significant regulated proteins, we then performed a network analysis with STRING and Cytoscape for visualizing potential protein-protein physical and/or genetic interactions.
Figure 3(A)
shows a virtual protein-protein interaction network of the 77 statistically significant proteins listed in
Table 2
. Some of these significant proteins, such as CAT, SERPINC1, SERPINB2, SERPINB5, IDH1, TIMP1, FCN3, MMP2, and SERPINA11, are associated with biological processes involved in oxidative stress, redox signaling, matrix remodeling, metallopeptidase, glycolysis, complement, peroxisome, lipid, blood coagulation, and fibrin clot formation.
Figure 3(B
,
C)
depict the network analysis of the statistically significant (
p
< 0.05) proteins in IUGR females and males listed in
Tables 3
and
4
, respectively. The heatmap of the top 15 most and least differentially abundant proteins are presented in
Figure 4(A)
for IUGR compared with AGA control whereas
Figure 4(B
,
C)
depict those for IUGR females and males, respectively, when compared with respective AGA controls. The hierarchal clustering of the top-ranked regulated proteins clearly showed that the proteins identified distinctly clustered into higher abundance and lower abundance profiles in IUGR versus AGA as well as when stratified by sex in IUGR female and male subjects versus their respective AGA controls. Finally, the heatmaps in
Figure 4
reveal similar changes in protein abundances associated with IUGR for the whole study population (
Figure 4A
) and for females (
Figure 4B
). The heatmap for males (
Figure 4C
), on the other hand, shows a distinct pattern, suggesting IUGR has a smaller effect on protein abundance in males than in females.
3.4 |
Metabolic risk proteins identified in IUGR cord blood
Furthermore, we assessed if metabolic risk proteins associated with obesity, type-2 diabetes, BMI, and glucose tolerance were detected among our statistically significantly differentially regulated proteins (
Table 5
). Several proteins such as TIMP1, SHBG, GLRX, and S100A8 were found to be most abundant in IUGR, and FCN3, MMP2, SERPINC1, ITIH1, and ITIH3, proteins associated with metabolic risk, were less abundant in IUGR (
Table 5
). Metabolic risk proteins EFEMP1, TGFBR3, GLRX, PCSK9, and S100A8 were highly abundant, while FCN3 and SERPINC1 were less abundant in IUGR females. In contrast, metabolic risk protein S100A10 was highly abundant and MMP2, LPL, RBP4, SERPINC1, and ITIH1 were less abundant in IUGR males. However, F9 and RBP4 are metabolic risk proteins unique to IUGR, whereas EFEMP1, PCSK9, and TGFBR3 are unique to IUGR females. Additional statistical analysis using two-way ANOVA also confirmed the latter three metabolic risk proteins to be significant for an interaction between Growth and Sex but not for either parameter alone (
Table S3
).
3.5 |
Increased catalase (CAT) activity in IUGR cord blood
We performed a functional validation catalase (CAT) assay using cord plasma from IUGR and AGA neonates based on the GO analyses, which indicated significant regulation of proteins involved in peroxisomal processes. As shown in
Figure 5(A)
, CAT is statistically significantly increased in IUGR compared to AGA. Interestingly, when stratified by sex, we observed increased CAT activity in IUGR females but not in males (
p
= 0.05;
Figure 5B
). In order to demonstrate whether there is a relationship between catalase abundance and activity, we quantified CAT abundance in IUGR versus AGA as well as based on sex stratification (
Figure 5C
,
D
). Our results revealed statistically significant differential abundance of CAT in IUGR compared to AGA as well as in IUGR females. Furthermore, we illustrated that CAT is a highly abundant protein using an MA plot with the log ratio between IUGR and AGA versus average protein abundance (
Figure 5E
).
3.6 |
Regression analysis
Finally, we performed multivariable regression for adjustment for covariates such as infant sex, ethnicity, preeclampsia/hypertension and maternal BMI affected CAT, AKR1B1, IDH1, GLRX, MMP2, and PAPPA2 levels (
Figure 5F
). In the univariate model, IUGR was positively associated with CAT, AKR1B1, IDH1, GLRX, and PAPPA2 and negatively associated with MMP2. The positive association between IUGR and CAT, AKR1B1, IDH1, and GLRX persisted after adjusting for infant sex, ethnicity, PE/HTN, and pre-pregnancy BMI. In contrast, the association between IUGR and MMP2 and PAPPA2 was no longer statistically significant after adjusting for these factors. PAPPA2 was positively associated with PE/HTN and pre-pregnancy BMI.
4 |
DISCUSSION
In this study, we provide a molecular understanding of the pathogenic mechanism(s) of IUGR and its consequences, including increased lifelong risk of metabolic disease, by comparing proteomic profiles of IUGR and AGA infants. In addition, to our knowledge, this is the first study demonstrating the influence of sex on mechanisms underlying IUGR pathogenesis. A major finding is that the proteins that exhibited the highest fold change in IUGR versus AGA are related to pathways associated with the peroxisome. The data suggest that changes in peroxisome pathways are critical in the pathogenesis of IUGR or, alternatively, may be one of the mechanisms by which the fetus responds to an adverse
in-utero
environment. However, other biological processes, such as electron transport chain and nucleotide metabolic and catabolic processes were also enriched, while the proteins that exhibited the lowest fold change in IUGR versus AGA were predominantly involved in platelet degranulation and aggregation, cell adhesion and regulation of response to stimulus. These findings agree with previous studies that identified platelet activation and extracellular matrix remodeling in fetal growth restriction [
21
].
Previous studies have demonstrated that IUGR alters the expression of proteins involved in the complement and coagulation process, lipid metabolism and transport, immune mechanisms, blood pressure and iron and copper homeostasis control. Dysfunction of several proteins such as nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate (NADPH) oxidase, alpha-1-antitrypsin (SERPINA1), insulin-like growth factor (IGF), matrix metalloproteinases and vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF), correlate with abnormal trophoblast invasion and vascular development, and oxidative stress in the placenta of IUGR subjects [
22
,
23
].
Several proteins identified in our cohort (e.g., CAT, HBG1, PKM, PNP, S100A8, IDH1) were previously reported to be associated with fetal growth restriction using either maternal or cord plasma [
12
,
15
,
21
]. IUGR is associated with impaired nutrient and/or oxygen delivery that may leave the mononuclear cells in cord plasma, fetal organs and placenta more susceptible to damage and leakage of cytosolic proteins consistent with the increased levels of proteins such as CAT in IUGR cord plasma [
12
,
15
,
24
,
25
]. In contrast to our findings, previous proteomics studies using cord blood have implicated lipoproteins such as Apolipoprotein C-II, Apolipoprotein C-III, and Apolipoprotein E in IUGR [
7
,
22
,
23
]. The difference in major proteomics signatures from our cohort may be due to differences in gestational age; the majority of IUGR cases in other reports were born preterm. Interestingly, some of these proteins were also detected at very low levels in our samples. Also, maternal plasma proteomic profiling revealed that most of the identified proteins in IUGR were associated with alterations in lipid metabolism [
10
]. Alterations in lipoproteins, along with LDL, can exhibit enhanced susceptibility to oxidation by free radicals. Previous studies from both rodents and humans support the idea of a crosstalk between mother and fetus related to lipid metabolism [
26
,
27
]. While in rodents the crosstalk is well established with mechanisms put forward, the human data supporting a cause and effect relationship has not as yet been established. Based on these findings, we hypothesize that alterations in maternal lipids can have an impact on fetal growth, thereby resulting in a compensatory response by the fetus as evidenced by increased redox signaling/peroxisome protein expression seen in the IUGR cord plasmas of our cohort. These results, therefore, suggest a critical role of oxidative stress in IUGR pathogenesis.
IUGR is a multifactorial, heterogeneous disease that, in some studies, has been shown to share similarities with preeclampsia (PE). Both IUGR and PE are placentally mediated disorders. Recent studies, however, have shown that IUGR and PE mechanisms are phenotypically distinct. A small proportion of mothers in our cohort were diagnosed with PE or gestational hypertension; some delivered AGA babies, while others delivered IUGR babies. This supports the notion that PE alone may not be directly associated with IUGR. Studies have identified protein signatures unique to only PE, most of which are related to complement and coagulation pathways [
28
]. Although some of these proteins, like C3, FCN3, ITIH1 and F9, overlap with our IUGR cohort, the major proteins in our cohort are distinct from PE, suggesting that our findings are likely not confounded by PE.
Furthermore, we observed that CAT protein abundance, an important peroxisomal enzyme activity, was significantly increased in cord plasma from IUGR compared to AGA neonates. Interestingly, CAT protein abundance was increased in IUGR females but unchanged in males. This finding is consistent with the hypothesis that IUGR affects female and male offspring differently [
16
–
18
]. To our knowledge, this is the first study to explore sex-related differences in proteomic profiles in IUGR cord blood. Sexual dimorphism was further evident in the CAT activity assay, where we observed a significant increase in CAT activity in female but not in male IUGR neonates. Overall, based on the proteomic profiles and CAT activity, our results agree with observations that, in response to an adverse developmental milieu, male infants have greater disadvantages during pregnancy. One possible explanation may be that the placenta of the female fetus protects them from adverse prenatal events [
29
]. This explanation is further evident in previous studies that showed that sex differences exist in clinical outcomes of various inflammatory disorders such as rheumatoid arthritis (RA) and sepsis [
30
–
32
].
Finally, the proteomic profiles of our cohort suggest our IUGR subjects are at increased risk of cardiometabolic disease. We identified some metabolic risk proteins associated with obesity (EFEMP1, TIMP1, S100A8, ITIH1, and ITIH3), type-2 diabetes/metabolic syndrome (IGFB2, FCN3, and TGFBR3), increased BMI (SERPINC1, IGFBP2, and SHBG), and glucose tolerance (GLRX and PCSK9), with a significant interaction of the growth and sex variables identified for EFEMP1, TGFBR3, and PSK9 in our significantly differentially abundant proteins in IUGR cord plasma [
33
–
38
].
Upregulation of TIMP1 and EFEMP1 in human plasma have been associated with obesity risk [
33
]; these proteins were detected among our significantly differentially expressed proteins and were also upregulated in IUGR cord plasma. In other studies, upregulation of LPL and SERPINC1 are associated with type 2 diabetes and BMI, respectively, which were also upregulated in IUGR in our study [
34
,
35
]. However, other studies show contradictory results in protein expression. For instance, in Ethadad et al. [
36
] upregulation of both MMP2 and FCN3 and down regulation of TGFBR3 and SHBG were associated with metabolic syndrome. These proteins were found to be opposite in their expression in our cohort study. The difference in expression pattern may be explained by proteins changing from birth to adulthood. Also, in Oller-Moreno et al. [
37
] upregulation of ITIH1 and downregulation of S100A8 are associated with risk of overweight. The expression patterns of these proteins are contrary to what is observed in IUGR cord blood at birth. Carrasco-Zanini et al. found GLRX, SHBG, F9, and C3 to be associated with risk of impaired glucose intolerance [
38
].
When we stratified our subjects based on sex, we identified proteins such as EFEMP1, PCSK9, and TGFBR3 to be metabolic risk proteins unique to IUGR females while F9 and RBP4 are unique to IUGR males. Interestingly, proteins such as EFEMP1 associated with obesity, PCSK9 associated with impaired glucose intolerance and TGFBR3 linked with metabolic syndrome were specific to female IUGR. Apart from being risk proteins, EFEMP1 and PCSK9 are linked to extracellular matrix remodeling [
39
] and PCSK9 is important in the regulation of cholesterol homeostasis [
40
]. TGFBR3 is a co-receptor that functions in cell proliferation, differentiation, and apoptosis [
41
].
On the other hand, F9 associated with pre-diabetes and RBP4 associated with impaired glucose intolerance are two metabolic risk proteins unique to IUGR males. F9 is a vitamin K-dependent plasma protein involved in blood coagulation processes [
42
] whereas RBP4 is a plasma membrane transporter vital in retinol metabolism. RBP4 is also associated with insulin resistance and adipose tissue dysfunction [
43
].
This is an observational study designed to identify associations between an IUGR phenotype and protein abundance in cord blood and thus cause and effect relationships cannot be assigned. The major strength of this study, however, is that we demonstrate sexually dimorphic outcomes in proteomic profiles of IUGR cord blood and identify metabolic risk proteins for future therapeutic targets. In addition, we have provided preliminary evidence that females respond better to IUGR insults than males. However, our study is limited by the small sample size and the lack of an independent cohort to validate the results. Future prospective studies with a greater number of subjects and longitudinal timepoints may identify additional risk biomarkers and whether the observed protein signatures result from placental dysfunction or fetal stress will provide deeper insights and improved therapeutics.
5 |
CONCLUSIONS
In summary, we showed that pathways related to the peroxisome may be associated with IUGR pathogenesis. The increase in oxidative stress/catalase activity we observed likely reflects a compensatory mechanism in response to the unfavorable inutero milieu. Interestingly, this effect displays sexual dimorphism with females showing more effective compensatory responses to IUGR than males. In addition, we identified metabolic risk proteins associated with obesity, type-2 diabetes, and glucose intolerance that were differentially expressed in IUGR cord blood. Taken together, our data reveal that the adverse in utero environments which result in IUGR also produce dramatic shifts in neonatal proteomic profiles with specific changes affecting oxidative stress and metabolism. Furthermore, responses to in utero allostatic stress show clear sexual dimorphism, which may be related to differences in lifelong risk for cardiometabolic disease between males and females.
